title: Make It Survive Reality
description: Your code works on your laptop. Now make it survive reality: figure out where every piece actually runs, what must survive a backend restart, which work belongs in the background, and what breaks when ten thousand people arrive at once.

objectives.label: Explain that deployment means deciding where each piece of the product runs and how it connects
Distinguish disposable compute from persistent state and place each where it belongs
Match each kind of work to the right pattern: fast request, background job or media delivery
Predict what a real system should do when a dependency fails or usage multiplies

lessons.title: Running is not the same as existing

blocks.text:
Ask a team where their project is and the first answers are GitHub, Replit, or my laptop. GitHub can hold the source. That is code existing. A process on a laptop is code running, and it stops when the lid closes. A product operating means several pieces keep serving people whether or not any one computer is awake.

Friday Night makes the gap concrete. It is a high-school sports app: clips, live scores, player tags, and an AI game summary. During the week one student runs it, five friends upload videos, and the summary appears. On championship night someone posts the link and ten thousand people open it, hundreds upload, and everyone asks for a summary. Software that works for five friends is not yet a system that works.

Deploy my app is not an instruction. The app is a frontend, a backend, a database, file storage, an AI service, background workers, and outside APIs. Deployment answers, for every piece: what is it, where does it run, how do other pieces reach it, what does it need, and what happens if it stops?

blocks.alt: A product broken into pieces: frontend, backend, database, file storage, AI service, background processing, notifications and external APIs, each of which may run somewhere different
blocks.caption: Deploy my app is not an instruction. The application is several different pieces, possibly on different machines in different companies, and deployment answers the same questions for each one.
steps: Frontend: the pages and components the browser loads
Backend: receives uploads, handles accounts, calls AI
File storage: the actual videos and photos
AI service: generates the game summaries
Background workers: compress video and make thumbnails
External APIs: maps, messaging, sports data

blocks.text:
The cloud is not one computer that runs the whole app. A phone reaches a frontend host. That host calls a backend. The backend reaches a database, object storage, and an AI API, and it may drop a job onto a queue that a video worker picks up. Those pieces can live on different machines, in different companies. The product works because each connection has a real address.

fridaynight.app is only the front door. It can point at the frontend. The frontend then calls something like api.fridaynight.app. The database, the storage bucket, and the queue should stay off the public internet. Connecting a domain does not finish deployment. It only tells people where the front door is.

A common failure is a frontend that loads and still calls http://localhost:8000. Localhost means this computer. After you deploy, this computer is the visitor's phone, and the team's backend is not on it. The development address has to become the production one, such as api.fridaynight.app.

blocks.question: The frontend deploys successfully and the site loads, but the Upload Video button does nothing. Inside the code is http://localhost:8000/upload. What is wrong?

options.label: The upload feature was never built
Localhost on the visitor's computer is not the team's backend — the frontend still points at a development address
The browser just needs a refresh

blocks.explanation: Localhost means this same computer. The deployed frontend now runs on every user's machine, and none of those machines hosts the team's backend on port 8000. The development address must become the production backend address, such as api.fridaynight.app.

blocks.title: Punchline
blocks.text: For every piece: what is it, where does it run, how do other pieces reach it, what does it need, and what happens if it stops?

slides.title: I delete your backend right now

blocks.text:
Delete the backend server this second. User accounts, game scores, and videos should still exist. What may disappear is the running process. You can start that code again on a new machine. Compute is disposable. Accounts, scores, and videos are state, and state has to survive the replacement.

The new process is useful only if it can find the old facts. It connects to the same database and the same file storage, and the product continues. If the videos lived in a folder on the machine you just deleted, the new process starts and the folder is empty.

Saving uploads to a folder inside the running backend is not a coding bug. The line can be correct, and the clip can play during the demo. It is an architecture bug, because the next backend starts empty.

blocks.title: The video and its record
steps: A student uploads state_championship_final_play.mp4, an 800 MB clip. The bytes and the description of those bytes do not belong in the same system.
The bytes go into object storage. The database is not a hard drive, and 50,000 videos should not be stuffed into ordinary rows. Storage contains the file.
The database keeps the record that knows about the file: video_id, user_id, game_id, filename, upload_time, processing_status, and storage_location.
One logical video may be several stored objects: the original, a 1080p copy, a 720p copy, and a thumbnail. The record points at each location.
Replace the backend and the new process reads that record, follows storage_location, and finds the same bytes. The record is how every piece finds the file after a restart.

blocks.question: The backend is replaced by a new machine. Which of these must still exist for the product to continue?

options.label: The database records and the files in object storage
The temporary variables from the last request

blocks.explanation: Compute is replaceable; state is not. Processes and request variables die with the machine by design, but accounts, scores and media must live in systems built to persist — the database and object storage — so a replacement backend can reconnect and continue.

slides.title: An architecture bug, not a coding bug

blocks.title: Punchline
blocks.text: Saving uploads to a folder inside the running backend is not a coding bug. It is an architecture bug — the next backend starts empty.

slides.title: Not all work is the same

blocks.text:
GET /game/123 reads one score and can return in about 50 milliseconds. POST /generate-summary sends facts to a model and may wait 5 to 20 seconds. POST /upload-video may accept a 500 MB clip, compress it, build several sizes, pull out the audio, make thumbnails, and run an analysis. That last job can take minutes.

Those are a fast request, a slow job, and heavy computation. If the upload request tries to finish the minutes of work before it answers, the student watches a spinner, the tab closes, the connection dies, and the operation can fail even though the file already arrived.

The upload should accept the file, record that processing has started, and return. The slow parts happen after that response. Forcing every job through one request shape is what makes the system fragile. Ask of every task: does the user need to wait for this?

slides.title: Do not make the user wait

blocks.alt: An upload flow that stores the video, marks it processing in the database, puts a job on a queue and responds immediately, while a separate worker compresses the video, creates thumbnails, runs AI analysis and marks it ready
blocks.caption: A queue is a list of work waiting to happen. A worker is a separate program that performs it. Ask of every task: does the user need to wait for this?
steps: User uploads video → the file is stored
Backend adds a job to the queue and responds immediately
A worker picks up the job
Worker compresses, creates thumbnails and runs AI analysis

blocks.text:
A queue is a list of work waiting to happen. A worker is a separate program that takes the next item and does it. They exist so the request that accepted the upload is not also the program that compresses the video.

The request stores the file, sets the record to processing, adds a job, and responds. The screen can move from Uploading to Processing. Later the worker compresses the clip, writes a thumbnail, runs the analysis, and sets the record to ready. If the browser is already closed, the worker still finishes, because that work was never tied to the open connection.

The same split fits any job the user does not have to watch finish: a PDF, 5,000 emails, an imported spreadsheet, or a batch of embeddings. If they do not need to wait, it can be background work.

slides.title: Big files take a different road

blocks.text:
A student in Tulsa uploads the winning play. Someone in Lawton watches it, someone in Oklahoma City watches it, and ten thousand people replay it. If every view goes through the backend, the backend downloads the 500 MB file from storage and sends it out again, once per viewer. That path is slow, it costs more, and it crowds out the requests that actually need the API, such as scores and accounts.

A content delivery network keeps copies of a file that many people request, closer to the people asking. The browser is given a file address and receives the bytes from that media system. The original still lives in object storage. The viewer's phone never has to pull the file through your application server.

The backend still decides who may watch and which address to hand out. The media system does the delivery. Frequently requested large files should not travel through the backend on every replay.

slides.title: Match the job to the shape

blocks.question: Processing an uploaded video takes several minutes. Where should that work happen?

options.label: Inside the upload request, so the user gets one complete answer
In the frontend, so the servers stay free
As a background job — the request accepts the upload, queues the work and responds immediately
In the database, so the work stays close to the data

blocks.explanation: A request that waits minutes risks dead connections and a locked-up backend. Accept the upload, record status = processing, enqueue the work and respond. A worker does the slow parts and updates the record when ready — the same pattern behind report generation, mass email and document analysis.

blocks.text:
Run the failures before championship night does. If the backend restarts and accounts disappear, state was stored on the disposable machine. If the AI provider stops responding, scores, video, and game pages should keep working, and the summary should say it is temporarily unavailable. One optional dependency should not take down the features that do not call it. That is graceful degradation.

A 40 GB upload is not a coat of polish on the form. The system needs a size limit, a check on the file type, and a bound on how much processing one file can start. Twenty thousand people watching one highlight may leave the database and the backend fine while video delivery is the piece that falls over. Different workloads stress different pieces.

Twenty thousand viewers who each trigger a new summary create twenty thousand identical model calls. Generate that summary once, store it, and reuse it. Ask what runs once, what runs per user, what runs per request, and what runs on every upload. Those questions are how architecture decides the bill. Kill the laptop. Kill the backend. Multiply users, files, AI calls, and traffic by one hundred. What breaks first is the next bottleneck.

blocks.question: On Friday night the AI summary provider stops responding. What should a resilient product do?

options.label: Show an error page for the whole site
Keep serving scores and video, and mark summaries temporarily unavailable
Wait silently until the provider comes back

blocks.explanation: One dependency failing should not sink features that do not need it. Graceful degradation returns everything the product can still provide and says clearly what is temporarily missing.

blocks.title: Punchline
blocks.text: Kill the laptop — does the product still run? Kill the backend — does anything important survive? Multiply users, files, AI calls and traffic by one hundred — what breaks first?

slides.title: The key that becomes a bill

blocks.text:
A student builds the summary feature and leaves the AI key in the frontend code. They publish the site. Someone finds the key, a script sends hundreds of thousands of requests, and the cloud bill arrives. The feature worked. The secret was in a place every browser can read.

Public facts can live in frontend code: the address of the site, the labels on the buttons. A database password, an AI key, an email key, and any private credential cannot. The browser should call your backend. Your backend calls the AI provider, and the key stays in the backend's environment or in a secret store. It does not go in the repository, and it does not ship to the browser.

The code says what it needs, for example AI_API_KEY. The environment says which value this running copy gets. Treat a variable like that as a slot, not as a mystery string pasted into the page.

slides.title: A joke in dev deletes the season

blocks.text:
In development, someone clicks Delete all games, laughs, and reloads the fake data. In production that same click can erase the season. Production changes the consequences: real people, real scores, real credentials, and changes you do not make casually. Development is fake data, local services, and frequent edits. A staging copy can sit between them so a new version is tried before real users see it.

The dangerous mix is development behavior aimed at production data. An agent can write a test that deletes rows. That test must not run against the database the live site uses. Development, preview, and production need separate configuration and separate databases.

The same code can do both, because the environment picks the target. DATABASE_URL points at the development database on a laptop and at the production database when the product is operating. You should be able to say exactly how the running copy knows which one it is.

Scaling is not a bigger server because more people showed up. Ten users work. A thousand users may still work. At 50,000, name the piece that fails. Maybe the backend cannot finish requests fast enough, so you add backend capacity. Then the database has too many connections. Then the AI provider rate-limits you. Then the video queue is twelve hours long, so you add workers. Then the bill is the thing that breaks.

Each fix reveals the next limit. Architecture for 50 users and architecture for 50 million users should not look the same. Building the giant version for a few hundred people spends complexity you do not need yet.

Say the scale you actually expect, and ask what would have to change if that number grew a hundred times. Make it scalable, with no number attached, is not an architecture.

slides.title: Know it failed, and be able to restore

blocks.text:
A student says the video disappeared. Without a log, that sentence is the whole record. With a log you can read the path: upload requested, user authenticated, record 8821 created, job created, worker started, then an error that the codec is unsupported. A shared request id can tie the frontend call, the backend call, the database write, the AI call, and the background job into one story. Ask where the request failed before you ask an agent to rewrite the feature.

Logs answer what happened. Monitoring answers whether the system is healthy right now: errors climbing, the backend silent, the queue growing, the disk nearly full, summaries failing. If the first news is an email that says the site has been down since yesterday, the users are the monitoring system.

Backups are the other catastrophe. At 2:13 someone deletes every game record. At 2:14 you need a copy you can actually restore. A backup that has never been restored is a hope, not a plan.
